newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: COFFEE--Rebels wreak havoc with Colombian exports.
newsitem.headline: COFFEE--Rebels wreak havoc with Colombian exports.

text.p: Coffee exporters have had to reschedule this month's shipments in the face of the continuing wave of leftist guerrilla attacks and highway blockades across Colombia.

"We have had to delay some shipments until the end of this month because of the (law and order) problems," said Gustavo Rivera, general manager of the storage and transport company Almacafe, part of the National Coffee Growers' Federation.

A four-week-old offensive by the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), the nation's largest guerrilla force, coupled with an "armed strike" or nationwide offensive declared by the second-biggest rebel force, the National Liberation Army (ELN), has periodically split the country in two and brought chaos to overland transport.

In a hint of what may lie ahead for coffee transporters and exporters when the harvest begins early next month, rebels have torched more than 30 tractor-trailers in various parts of the country in the past month, particularly along the highways leading to the Caribbean coast ports.

The guerrilla action has completely halted coal shipments out of Santa Marta in northern Magdalena province, Colombian radio reported on Wednesday. Last Friday, 17 coal trucks and their cargoes were set ablaze by ELN rebels en route from mines in northern Cesar province to the port.

About 45 percent of Colombia's export quality coffee is shipped out through Santa Marta or Cartagena, also in Magdalena province. The remainder is moved out through Buenaventura, on Colombia's southwest Pacific coast.
Transporters problems have been exacerbated by insurers' refusal to consider any claims for damage to trucks caused during the ELN's armed strike, scheduled to last until September 30.

There are no official estimates of how many coffee-carrying trucks have been hit in the latest spiral of violence, but firefights have been reported in at least two central coffee- growing provinces. Rivera said all eyes were now focused on what may happen at the end of this month, one of the busiest times for coffee shipments.
The situation could become even more critical as the main harvest -- 60 percent of total production -- gets under way in early October.
"It's not the price of coffee that's bothering us but rather that we may default on some export deliveries," said one private exporter, who did not wish to be named.

He said that guerrilla blockades on main highways could cause delays of between three to five days while the security forces regained control of the situation and cleared burned out vehicles from stretches of road.
"That would be fatal for us especially in such a competitive market as this," the exporter said.
For every tractor-trailor, with a small cargo of 240 154-lb (70 kg) bags of export grade coffee, burned by the guerrillas, companies stand to lose $43,000.
"Just imagine if they hit three or four trucks with larger loads," the exporter said.

"There are grave concerns about guerrillas within the sector because they're not bothered what grade coffee we're hauling, they just set it on fire. It's a strategy designed to sow panic," another private exporter added.

In addition to the turbulent climate of law and order, coffee producers and exporters are facing a second problem -- the rising value of the peso against the dollar. Domestic costs have risen while potential export profits are being pushed down.
